title: Choose Europe for Science: over 100 national and regional initiatives aim to attract global research talent
date_evidence: News article - 30 January 2026 - Directorate-General for Research and Innovation ... Publication date 30 January 2026 (Last updated on: 2 February 2026)
key_claim: Europe now offers 101 national and regional schemes to attract research talent (up from 65 in May 2025), backed by nearly EUR 900 million in EU funding. Since Choose Europe launched, applications from researchers based outside Europe or associated countries for ERC Advanced Grants have nearly quadrupled (168 vs 45), Starting Grants rose more than 50% (246 vs 159), the Consolidator 2026 call rose 130% (115 vs 50) and MSCA postdoctoral fellowships rose 65%. Concrete results: Germany's Global Minds programmes selected 166 researchers in H2 2025, Austria's APART-USA awarded 25 fellowships, France's Safe Place for Science at Aix-Marseille selected around 60, and VUB Brussels recruited 12.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): canonical primary source for the European pull-factor framing and the ERC application-surge data.

title: NRMP Releases Results of the 2026 Main Residency Match for More Than 38,000 Future Residents
key_claim: In the 2026 Main Residency Match, foreign-born international medical graduates requiring visa sponsorship had a PGY-1 match rate of 54.4 percent, a five-year low, compared with 67.9 percent for foreign-born IMGs not requiring sponsorship (US permanent residents), a five-year high. Non-US citizen IMGs numbered 11,944 active applicants, up 479 from 2025, with an overall PGY-1 match rate of 56.4 percent, the lowest in five years.
verbatim_quote: foreign-born IMGs requiring visa sponsorship had a PGY-1 match rate of 54.4 percent, a five-year low, compared with 67.9 percent for foreign-born IMGs not requiring sponsorship (U.S. permanent residents), a five-year high.
notes: Primary-data leading indicator: immigration friction visible in disaggregated visa-sponsorship match rates. Also carries counter-evidence (non-US IMG applicants still rising).

title: Business Coalition Warns Research Funding Chaos Is Fueling New U.S. Brain Drain
date_evidence: April 17, 2026 ... Business Coalition Warns Research Funding Chaos Is Fueling New U.S. Brain Drain
key_claim: A report by Business for Federal Research Funding (a coalition of 80+ chambers of commerce) summarises initiatives from 21 nations plus the EU to lure US-based researchers abroad, and reports losses of early-career and experienced researchers in more than half of US states. Examples: Canada's C$1.7bn Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative (1,000+ researchers); France's Choose France for Science (46 awards, 41 to people previously at US institutions); named institutional losses including Colorado State (to Austria), MIT (Canada), University of Central Florida (Japan) and University of Alaska-Fairbanks (Sweden), plus NASA, the national labs, NIH, NSF and Mayo Clinic. Programmes often offer support for up to 10 years and expedited visas in as little as a month.
notes: Tier 2 institutional reporting on the BFRF coalition report; documents the breadth (21 nations) and the multi-year lock-in structure of recruitment packages.

title: The Cost of the Trump Administration's Attacks on Research Funding
key_claim: American scientists submitted 32% more applications to jobs abroad in the year to early 2026 than in the same period a year earlier; 85 rising and established US scientists, including an NIH neurobiologist and a Princeton nuclear physicist, moved to China in the past year; Chinese universities have begun to displace US institutions in global research output. The FY2027 budget request again seeks deep cuts (NIH 13%, NSF 55%), even though Congress largely rejected the FY2026 cuts and courts blocked the mass funding freeze.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank brief; supplies the China dimension, the applications-abroad quantum, and the strongest counter-evidence (Congressional and judicial pushback).

title: Resources on American Researchers Leaving the United States
date_evidence: Association of American Universities April 2026 Page 1 of 4 RESOURCES ON AMERICAN RESEARCHERS LEAVING THE UNITED STATES
key_claim: A standing AAU compilation (April 2026 edition) of departures and recruitment moves, including: Harvard, Dartmouth and Cornell academics departing for an Australian university (Boston Globe, 24/02/2026); two Nobel Prize-winning economists leaving the US for Zurich (Inside Higher Ed, 15/10/2025); China pledging a billion-dollar science spending boost (Nature, 11/03/2026); and dozens of researchers moving to France from the US (Nature, 10/02/2026).
notes: Tier 2 compilation evidencing named senior-level departures (Nobel laureates, cohorts to Australia) - corroborates that the outflow reaches elite tiers, not only early career.

title: National survey of NIH-funded researchers shows precarious state of U.S. science
date_evidence: By Jonathan Wosen March 19, 2026 ... A nationwide STAT survey of federally funded researchers
key_claim: In a STAT/MassINC survey of 989 NIH-funded researchers (fielded 28 Jan-18 Feb 2026), 13% said their labs had lost researchers to institutions in other countries; 29% of tenure-track researchers had applied for jobs at other institutions (nearly twice the 15% rate among tenured faculty); 53% are advising students to consider positions outside the US; and only 35% of those whose grants were cut or delayed had funding fully restored by end-2025.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism reporting primary survey data on the push side of the outflow.

title: Immigration changes are driving foreign researchers to leave the U.S. - or not come to begin with
date_evidence: By Andrew Joseph May 4, 2026 ... New data suggest America is becoming a less attractive destination
key_claim: 14% of surveyed NIH-funded researchers said immigration policy changes forced scientists, students or postdocs to turn down offers to work in their labs, and 13% lost researchers to other countries; the 2026 Match rate for visa-needing international graduates hit a five-year low. Counter-evidence: the number of non-citizen international medical graduates applying to US residencies still rose 4.2%, and interviewees said the US is 'still the land of opportunity'.
notes: Tier 3; supplies the immigration-friction mechanism and the strongest sourced counter-evidence (inbound demand still rising).
